title: K-R-A
hook: kara: to call and to read; Mikra, scripture, is "what is called out"

segments.voice: Yesterday, D-B-R: davar, a word and a thing at once, and the same letters inside midbar, the wilderness. Your line was words are things. Did your word become a deed? Today, a new week, and a root you can hear. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

An old letter from a grandmother turns up in a drawer. Nobody in the family reads it alone. Someone unfolds it, clears their throat, and reads it out to the whole room, and the room goes quiet to listen. Reading like that isn't silent. It's something done with the voice, and it's aimed at somebody. Hebrew keeps that close. In Hebrew the verb to read and the verb to call are the same verb, from one root. Kuf, resh, alef: K-R-A.
screen: `A LETTER FROM A DRAWER.` → `READ OUT TO THE ROOM.` → `K-R-A: TO CALL, TO READ.`

segments.voice: Turn kara four ways. First, calling. The book known in English as Leviticus opens, "And the LORD called unto Moses." In Hebrew the first word is vayikra, and he called, and that word became the book's Hebrew name: Vayikra. A whole book that begins with a call. Second, calling out. In Isaiah's vision, the prophet sees the seraphim standing above the throne, "And one called unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts." Called, again: kara. Not whispered. Called, so the one across can hear. Third, reading. Much later, in the book of Nehemiah, the people gather in a square in Jerusalem. Ezra the scribe opens the book of the Torah, and when he opens it, all the people stand up. Then, the text says, "they read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." The reading, there, is mikra. Fourth, the name. Mikra became one of the Jewish names for the Bible itself: what is read, what is called out. Not a book you take to your room and read alone. A book read aloud, to people standing in a square, with someone beside it explaining. In synagogues to this day the Torah is read aloud from the scroll, and people are called up to stand beside it. So put the two meanings together. To call is to aim your voice at someone. To read, in Hebrew, is to do the same thing with a page. Whoever read that letter out to the room already knew it: reading is calling.
screen: `VAYIKRA: AND HE CALLED.` · `ONE CALLED UNTO ANOTHER: HOLY.` · `EZRA OPENS THE BOOK; THEY STAND.` · `MIKRA: WHAT IS CALLED OUT.` · then, large: `קָרָא`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse aloud. Settle, and breathe. On the screen is the line from Isaiah, the angels calling to each other. Read it once in your head. Now read it out loud, slowly, as if someone across the room needs to hear it. Holy, holy, holy. Notice what changes when the words leave your mouth: the pace, the breath, the weight. Then let the room go quiet again and sit with the echo. If you'd rather, read any verse you love the same way. The bell holds the time.
screen: `AND ONE CALLED UNTO ANOTHER, AND SAID:`
`HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, IS THE LORD OF HOSTS.`

segments.voice: K-R-A. Kuf, resh, alef: kara, to call and to read; mikra, scripture, what is called out. Today's word.
Your line: reading is calling. Today, read one thing aloud to someone else, a verse, a recipe, a paragraph, and watch them listen. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll, and members of the congregation are called up to stand beside it; Jews call the book known in English as Leviticus Vayikra, from its first word.

pairs: opened the book in the square

myth: in Hebrew, to call and to read come from the same root
in Isaiah's vision, the seraphim whisper to each other
"one called unto another": kara, aloud, so the other can hear.
in Nehemiah, the people read the Torah silently, each alone
Ezra reads aloud in a square, and the reading is explained so they understand.

fork.setup: you're in the square in Jerusalem. Ezra the scribe stands up high and opens the book of the Torah. what do the people do?
fork.reveal: when he opens the book, all the people stand. then it's read aloud, distinctly, and explained.

original.note: Hebrew: he called, he read; the root of mikra, scripture.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading is something you do silently, alone.
what it means: in Hebrew, kara means both to call and to read.
what a scholar hears: Nehemiah 8:8 already calls the public reading mikra, a name later used for scripture.

notes: Editor: replaced the child-reading hook (day 1383 had a child on a rug) with a grandmother's letter read aloud; 'angels' changed to 'the seraphim' as Isaiah 6 says; replaced the Leviticus-name myth item, which repeated day 1386's Deuteronomy-name item.
Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Leviticus 1:1, Isaiah 6:3 and Nehemiah 8:8 as quoted.
Nehemiah 8:8: 'the reading' = bamikra. Confirm. Nehemiah 8:1-5 paraphrased (square before the water gate; Ezra opens the book; all stand).
'Mikra became one of the Jewish names for the Bible' and 'people are called up to stand beside it' (aliyah, though aliyah is from a different root) are descriptions of Jewish usage; confirm.
